course.title: The Lean Startup
course.description: The lean startup method is a way to build new companies and products under extreme uncertainty, testing a vision through fast, cheap experiments instead of long guesswork. This course adapts its structure from the Lean startup article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), and draws on the work of Eric Ries and Steve Blank. You will learn validated learning, the Build-Measure-Learn loop, the minimum viable product, customer development, pivots, innovation accounting, and the Lean Canvas, along with where the approach fits and where it does not.

questions.prompt: What problem does the lean startup method mainly address?
questions.explanation: Eric Ries framed lean startup as management for new ventures facing extreme uncertainty, not steady, predictable work.

questions.prompt: 'Validated learning' means progress shown by...
questions.explanation: Progress is measured by what you learn about customers from real tests, not by activity or output alone.

questions.prompt: The Build-Measure-Learn loop begins by turning an idea into...
options: a product or experiment you can measure
questions.explanation: You build something testable, measure how customers respond, and learn whether the idea holds - then repeat the loop.

questions.prompt: A minimum viable product (MVP) is best described as...
options: the cheapest possible product of low quality
the smallest thing that lets you start learning from customers
a product with every planned feature
a free version given away forever
questions.explanation: An MVP is the least effort needed to begin the learning loop, not simply a cheap or unfinished product.

questions.prompt: 'Get out of the building', associated with Steve Blank, tells founders to...
options: work longer hours at their desks
test assumptions by talking to real customers outside
avoid speaking to users until launch
questions.explanation: Steve Blank's customer development urges founders to test guesses against real people in the market, not inside the office.

questions.prompt: A 'pivot' is...
options: a structured change in strategy that keeps the vision
questions.explanation: A pivot is a deliberate course correction to test a new fundamental hypothesis, not abandonment of the venture.

questions.prompt: 'Vanity metrics' are numbers that...
options: look impressive but do not guide decisions
questions.explanation: Vanity metrics flatter without informing; actionable metrics tie cause to effect and guide the next move.

questions.prompt: The Lean Canvas is...
options: a one-page model of a business and its riskiest parts
questions.explanation: The Lean Canvas is a single-page sketch of problem, solution, customers, and risks, adapted from the Business Model Canvas.

lessons.title: What the lean startup is and why it exists
lessons.grammar_note: Throughout this course, 'startup' means any team building something new under uncertainty, not a company defined by its size or age.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the lean startup method is, where it came from, and why it exists. By the end of this lesson you will be able to say, in plain language, why building something new under uncertainty calls for a different kind of management than running a stable, predictable business. Warm-up from the diagnostic: what main problem does the method address? Hold on to that answer, extreme uncertainty, because every tool in this course is a direct response to it. A startup, in this tradition, does not mean a small or young company measured by headcount or age. It means any team working to create a new product or service when the outcome is genuinely unknown. That broad definition, which Eric Ries helped make popular, is what lets the same ideas apply inside a two-person garage project and inside a large, established firm trying to launch something it has never sold before.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For most of the twentieth century, management meant planning: forecast the market, write a detailed plan, then execute it well. That works when the future resembles the past. Startups live in the opposite world, where customers, pricing, and even the problem itself are uncertain. Eric Ries, drawing on lean manufacturing from Toyota and on the customer development work of his mentor Steve Blank, argued that the right response is not better forecasting but faster learning. The lean startup treats a new venture as a set of untested guesses about the world. Instead of spending months perfecting a product no one may want, the team runs small, quick experiments to discover what is actually true. The goal is to find a sustainable business model before the money runs out. Waste, in this view, is any effort that does not teach you something about what customers truly value. The method exists because so many new products fail not from poor engineering but from building something nobody needed.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Three ideas anchor the method. First, a startup is an institution for creating value under extreme uncertainty, so its core skill is managing that uncertainty. Second, progress is measured by validated learning: evidence from real customers, not lines of code or hours worked. Third, learning happens through a repeating cycle of Build, Measure, and Learn. Consider a team convinced that busy parents want a meal-planning service. The planning instinct is to build the full app over a year. The lean instinct is to ask: what is the single riskiest assumption here? Probably that parents will pay for planning at all. So the team might offer a simple weekly plan by email to fifty families and watch whether anyone signs up or pays. Within two weeks they learn more than a year of internal debate would reveal. Zappos famously tested whether people would buy shoes online by photographing shoes in local stores before holding any inventory, a cheap test of a very costly assumption.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these and check yourself against the answers. 1) In one sentence, what makes something a startup in this sense? 2) Name the manufacturing tradition the method borrows from. 3) Who are the two people most associated with lean startup thinking? 4) Why is a long, detailed plan risky for a startup? 5) What counts as 'waste' in this framework? Answers: 1) A team creating a new product or service under extreme uncertainty, whatever its size or age. 2) Lean manufacturing, developed at Toyota. 3) Eric Ries, who wrote The Lean Startup, and Steve Blank, who developed customer development. 4) Because the plan rests on untested assumptions, and in uncertainty those are often wrong, so months of work can go toward a product nobody wants. 5) Any effort that does not produce learning about what customers truly value.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'lean' as a synonym for cheap or small. Lean is about speed of learning and cutting waste, not about spending as little as possible; a well-funded team can still be lean. Mistake: assuming the method only suits software ventures. The same logic guides new offerings in food, hardware, services, and large firms. Mistake: believing lean means no planning. You still form a clear vision and strategy; you just hold specific assumptions loosely and test them. Mistake: measuring success by effort rather than by what customers do. Exit ticket: (a) What does the method measure progress by? (b) Why does the method exist at all? Answers: validated learning, meaning evidence gathered from real customers; it exists because most new products fail from building things nobody wants, and faster learning reduces that risk.

lessons.title: Validated learning and the Build-Measure-Learn loop
lessons.grammar_note: Plan the Build-Measure-Learn loop backward - start from what you need to learn, not from what you want to build.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define validated learning and walk through the Build-Measure-Learn loop in order. You will be able to take a vague product idea and describe the first small experiment that would teach you the most. Warm-up: in the diagnostic, where does the loop begin, with a finished product or with something you can measure? The loop begins with building the smallest testable thing. By the end you should see why a startup's real output is not the product itself but the validated knowledge it gains about customers. That shift in what counts as progress is the heart of the method, and it is what separates busywork from genuine advancement when the future is unclear. Keep asking: what did we actually learn this week, and how do we know it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Validated learning is progress proven by data from real customers rather than by opinion, hope, or activity. A team can feel productive while building features nobody uses; validated learning asks, instead, what have we actually confirmed about our customers and their behavior? Eric Ries describes the engine of this learning as the Build-Measure-Learn loop. You start with an idea, build a minimum product or experiment, measure how real people respond, and learn whether your assumption held. Then you decide what to do next and go around again. Crucially, you plan the loop in reverse: first decide what you need to learn, then what to measure to know it, then the smallest thing to build that produces that measurement. Speed around the loop matters more than any single pass, because the team that learns fastest, at the lowest cost, is the one most likely to find a working model before its resources run out.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: The loop has three stops. Build: create the least you can to test one assumption. Measure: gather real behavioral data, not just stated opinions. Learn: compare the data to your hypothesis and decide. Imagine a team that believes commuters want an app that summarizes the news in five minutes. Working backward, the learning goal is 'will commuters listen daily?' The measure is daily return visits among a trial group. The build is a bare-bones feed of five short clips, released to a hundred commuters. If only a handful return after the first day, the team has learned something valuable and cheaply. Compare that to the alternative: a year spent building a polished app with social features, offline mode, and recommendations, only to discover the core daily habit never formed. Dropbox used a simple demonstration video as its build step, measuring sign-ups to a waiting list to confirm real demand before finishing the product.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In your own words, what is validated learning? 2) List the three stages of the loop in order. 3) In what order do you plan the loop? 4) Why does speed around the loop matter? 5) For a dog-walking booking service, name one learning goal and one thing you could measure. Answers: 1) Progress demonstrated by real evidence from customers, not by effort or opinion. 2) Build, then Measure, then Learn. 3) In reverse: decide what to learn, then what to measure, then what to build. 4) Because faster, cheaper loops mean more chances to find a working model before the money runs out. 5) Learning goal: will owners book a walk through the service at least weekly? Measure: the number of repeat bookings in the first two weeks among trial users.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: measuring activity instead of learning, counting features shipped or hours worked rather than what customers did. Mistake: planning the loop forward by starting with a big build. Start from the learning goal and shrink the build to fit it. Mistake: treating one loop as the whole story; the power lies in repeating quickly, each pass sharpening your understanding. Mistake: confusing opinions with evidence. A survey where people say they would pay is far weaker than watching them actually pay. Exit ticket: (a) What is the correct planning order for the loop? (b) What is a startup's true output, according to Ries? Answers: decide what to learn, then what to measure, then what to build; its true output is validated learning about customers, which the product is merely a means to produce.

lessons.title: The minimum viable product
lessons.grammar_note: Minimum viable product is minimal in effort-before-learning, not in quality - it is the least you can build to test your riskiest assumption.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a minimum viable product is, what it is not, and how to choose one for a given assumption. You will be able to list several types of MVP and match each to the kind of question it answers. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, is an MVP simply the cheapest, lowest-quality version of a product? No, it is the smallest version that lets you start the learning loop. By the end you should be comfortable designing an MVP that tests your riskiest assumption with the least possible effort, and you should understand why releasing it early, even when it feels embarrassing, usually beats polishing in private. The aim is not to impress; the aim is to learn what real customers actually do when the product is in front of them.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A minimum viable product is the version of a new product that lets a team collect the greatest amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort. The emphasis falls on learning, not on being cheap or incomplete for its own sake. The MVP exists to answer a specific question: will customers behave the way we assume? Eric Ries stresses that the first version will feel unfinished, and that founders often resist shipping it because it lacks features they are proud of. But every feature added before you have evidence is a bet placed blind. The discipline is to strip the product down to the single assumption you most need to test, release it to real customers, and let their behavior teach you. If the core assumption fails, all those unbuilt features would have been wasted effort anyway. An MVP is a way of starting the conversation with the market, not the final word in it.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: MVPs come in many shapes. A concierge MVP delivers the service by hand, with no automation, so the team learns whether people want it at all. A Wizard of Oz MVP looks automated to the customer but is run manually behind the scenes. A landing-page MVP describes the offer and measures how many visitors sign up or pre-order. A single-feature product does one thing to test the core value. Food on the Table began as a concierge service: the founder personally planned meals and shopped with a few families before writing any software. Zappos tested demand by listing shoes without holding stock. The choice of MVP follows the question. If the risk is 'does anyone want this?', a landing page or concierge test is enough. If the risk is 'can we deliver it reliably?', a Wizard of Oz test fits better. Always pick the cheapest MVP that still answers your riskiest question honestly, and define in advance what a pass or fail would look like.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Define an MVP in one sentence. 2) True or false: an MVP must be low quality. 3) Match the risk to a test: you are unsure anyone wants your idea at all. 4) What is a Wizard of Oz MVP? 5) Why does Ries say the first version should feel almost embarrassing? Answers: 1) The smallest version of a product that lets you gather the most validated learning with the least effort. 2) False - it is minimal in scope for learning, not necessarily low in quality; it simply omits everything not needed to test the key assumption. 3) A landing-page or concierge MVP that measures real interest before you build the full thing. 4) A product that appears automated to customers while people perform the work by hand behind the scenes. 5) Because if it already feels fully finished, you have probably built too much before testing whether anyone wants it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating minimum with shoddy. An MVP can be high quality in the one dimension being tested while leaving everything else out. Mistake: adding 'just one more feature' before release, which delays learning and raises the cost of being wrong. Mistake: building an MVP with no clear question attached, so you cannot tell what the result means. Mistake: ignoring the result because it is uncomfortable; the whole point of the test is to listen. Exit ticket: (a) What does the M in MVP really minimize? (b) Name one MVP type and the question it answers. Answers: it minimizes the effort spent before you begin learning, not the product's worth; a concierge MVP, delivered by hand, answers whether people want the service at all before you automate it.

questions.prompt: In the lean startup, progress is best measured by...
options: the size of the funding round
questions.explanation: Validated learning, evidence of real customer behavior, is the true measure, not activity or output.

questions.prompt: You should plan the Build-Measure-Learn loop...
options: in reverse, starting with what to learn
questions.explanation: Decide the learning goal first, then the measure, then the smallest build that produces it.

questions.prompt: A minimum viable product is designed mainly to...
options: maximize learning with the least effort
questions.explanation: An MVP gathers the most validated learning for the least effort, testing the riskiest assumption.

questions.prompt: A concierge MVP works by...
options: fully automating the service from day one
delivering the service manually to a few customers
questions.explanation: A concierge MVP delivers the service by hand first, so the team learns whether people want it before building software.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest evidence that customers value an offer?
options: people say in a survey they would pay
people actually sign up or pay
the team feels confident about it
competitors already exist in the market
questions.explanation: Observed behavior, such as paying or signing up, beats stated intentions, which often do not predict action.

questions.prompt: The two thinkers most associated with the method are...
questions.explanation: Eric Ries built on Steve Blank's customer development to formulate the lean startup.

lessons.title: Customer development, hypotheses, and experiments
lessons.grammar_note: A useful hypothesis is falsifiable: it names a specific threshold, set in advance, that a real result can fail to meet.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe customer development and the habit of getting out of the building, and turn a vague belief into a testable hypothesis with a clear experiment. You will be able to write a leap-of-faith assumption as a specific, falsifiable statement and design a test for it. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, where does Steve Blank say the facts about your business live? Outside the building, with real customers, not in your office or your spreadsheet. By the end you should treat your business plan as a stack of guesses to be checked against the world, and you should know how to check the guesses that matter most, first. This habit of listing assumptions and ranking them by risk is what keeps a team from quietly building on top of a false belief for months.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Steve Blank developed customer development as a counterpart to product development. While engineers build the product, founders must discover and validate who the customer is and what they need. His blunt instruction, get out of the building, captures the whole stance: the answers are not inside your head or your office, they are with the people you hope to serve. Eric Ries folded this into the lean startup through hypotheses and experiments. Every business plan rests on leap-of-faith assumptions, the beliefs that must be true for the venture to work. The two biggest are usually the value hypothesis, that customers will find the product valuable, and the growth hypothesis, that it will spread to new customers. A good experiment turns one assumption into a prediction specific enough to be proven wrong, then gathers real data to see whether that prediction survives contact with actual customers.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Start by listing your leap-of-faith assumptions and ranking them by risk: which, if false, would sink the whole idea? Rewrite the riskiest as a falsifiable hypothesis, not 'students like our tutoring' but 'at least thirty percent of students who try a free session book a paid one within a week.' Now design the smallest experiment that tests it, defining in advance what result would count as a pass or a fail. Get out of the building to run it: interview users, watch them use an early version, or offer the real thing to a small group. Blank distinguishes customer discovery, finding who has the problem, from customer validation, confirming they will pay to solve it. For a language-tutoring idea, discovery might be twenty interviews with learners about their real frustrations; validation might be selling ten actual sessions. Each step replaces opinion with evidence drawn from the market itself rather than from the team's hopes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does 'get out of the building' mean, and who is it from? 2) Name the two main leap-of-faith assumptions. 3) Rewrite this as a falsifiable hypothesis: 'people will like our app.' 4) What must you define before running an experiment? 5) Distinguish customer discovery from customer validation. Answers: 1) Test your assumptions by talking to and observing real customers rather than guessing from your desk; it comes from Steve Blank. 2) The value hypothesis, that customers find the product valuable, and the growth hypothesis, that it reaches new customers. 3) For example: 'at least twenty percent of new users return to the app three days after signing up.' 4) What result will count as success and what will count as failure, decided in advance. 5) Discovery finds who has the problem and what they need; validation confirms they will actually pay for your solution.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: asking leading questions that fish for the answer you want instead of letting customers surprise you. Mistake: writing hypotheses too vaguely to fail, such as 'customers will love it,' which no result can disprove. Mistake: skipping customer discovery and jumping straight to building, so you end up validating a problem nobody has. Mistake: running a test without deciding beforehand what pass and fail look like, which lets you rationalize any outcome. Exit ticket: (a) What makes a hypothesis useful for an experiment? (b) What is the difference between the value and growth hypotheses? Answers: it must be specific and falsifiable, with a clear threshold you set in advance; the value hypothesis asks whether customers find the product worthwhile, while the growth hypothesis asks whether and how it will reach more customers.

lessons.title: Pivot or persevere, and innovation accounting
lessons.grammar_note: A pivot changes the strategy but keeps the vision; perseverance keeps both. Neither is the same as quitting.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the pivot-or-persevere decision and describe innovation accounting with actionable metrics. You will be able to tell a pivot from a mere feature change, and an actionable metric from a vanity metric. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, is a pivot the same as giving up? No, it is a structured change of strategy that keeps the larger vision intact. By the end you should be able to look at a dashboard of numbers and say which ones would actually change a decision, and you should understand how teams hold themselves accountable for learning when traditional profit-and-loss figures are still near zero. This matters because attachment to an original plan, flattered by numbers that only ever rise, is one of the most common ways a promising venture quietly wastes its runway.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: After each turn of the loop, a startup faces one question: pivot or persevere? To persevere is to keep the current strategy and keep tuning it. To pivot is to make a structured change to one part of the strategy while keeping the vision fixed, perhaps a new customer segment, a new problem, or a new revenue model. Eric Ries lists many kinds, such as the zoom-in pivot, where a single feature becomes the whole product, and the customer-segment pivot, where the product fits a different buyer than planned. Teams persevere far too long when they rely on flattering numbers. Innovation accounting is the discipline that corrects this. It sets up a baseline from a first MVP, tunes the engine toward an ideal, and then judges honestly whether that tuning is moving the real drivers of the business. Without it, a team cannot reliably tell genuine learning apart from wishful thinking.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Innovation accounting leans on actionable metrics and warns against vanity metrics. A vanity metric, such as total registered users or cumulative downloads, almost always rises and so always looks good, yet it rarely tells you what to do next. An actionable metric ties a clear cause to an effect and can guide a decision. Cohort analysis is a favorite tool: instead of lumping all users together, you track each weekly group of newcomers separately and watch whether, say, the share who become paying customers improves as you change the product. Suppose conversions sit flat at two percent across many cohorts despite steady work; that flat line is a strong signal to consider a pivot. A famous example is Groupon, which pivoted from a stalled collective-action site called The Point into daily deals once that narrower idea showed real traction, a zoom-in pivot that kept the founders' broader vision alive.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Define a pivot in one sentence. 2) Give one example of a named pivot type. 3) What is the difference between a vanity metric and an actionable metric? 4) Why is cohort analysis useful? 5) What is the point of innovation accounting? Answers: 1) A structured change to part of the strategy that keeps the core vision, made to test a new fundamental hypothesis. 2) The zoom-in pivot, where one feature becomes the entire product, or the customer-segment pivot, among others. 3) A vanity metric looks good and tends only to rise but does not guide action, while an actionable metric links cause to effect and can change a decision. 4) It separates each group of new users over time, so you can see whether product changes truly improve behavior rather than hiding it inside one big total. 5) To hold a team honestly accountable for learning and to make the pivot-or-persevere call on evidence rather than hope.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling every small change a pivot; adjusting a button color is tuning, not a change of strategy. Mistake: trusting vanity metrics because they always climb, which hides a stalled business behind a rising line. Mistake: persevering out of attachment to the original plan rather than out of evidence. Mistake: judging a young venture only by its current profit, which innovation accounting replaces with clear learning milestones. Exit ticket: (a) What stays the same in a pivot and what changes? (b) Name one property of an actionable metric. Answers: the vision stays the same while a specific part of the strategy changes; an actionable metric links a clear cause to an effect and can be acted on, often examined through cohorts rather than through totals.

lessons.title: The Lean Canvas, and where lean fits and its limits
lessons.grammar_note: Lean startup manages market uncertainty with fast, cheap tests - it is strongest when experiments are quick and safe, and weakest when they are not.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Lay out a Lean Canvas for an idea and judge honestly where the lean startup approach fits well and where it does not. You will be able to name the riskiest boxes on the canvas and explain situations in which rapid experimentation is a poor guide. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, how long is a Lean Canvas? One page. By the end you should be able to sketch a business on a single sheet in a few minutes, use it to decide what to test first, and also recognize the honest limits of the method so that you neither overuse it nor dismiss it, but apply it where fast, cheap learning actually reduces real uncertainty. A tool is only useful when you know the problems it was built for and the problems it was not.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Lean Canvas, created by Ash Maurya and adapted from Alexander Osterwalder's Business Model Canvas, replaces the long business plan with a single page of nine boxes: problem, customer segments, unique value proposition, solution, channels, revenue streams, cost structure, key metrics, and unfair advantage. Its purpose is speed and risk-spotting: you fill it in quickly, then ask which boxes are guesses rather than facts. Those guesses become your first experiments. The canvas pairs naturally with everything in this course, because it makes the leap-of-faith assumptions visible at a glance. Yet the lean startup is not a universal law. It shines where uncertainty is high and experiments are cheap and fast. It strains where a single test would cost years or lives, where the vision depends on one long, indivisible bet, or where customers simply cannot react in a meaningful way to an early, partial version of the product.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Fill a Lean Canvas for a bike-repair-at-home service: problem, broken bikes and no time; segment, urban commuters; value proposition, repairs at your door within a day; solution, mobile mechanics; channels, local social posts and flyers; revenue, a per-repair fee; costs, mechanic time and a van; key metric, repeat bookings; unfair advantage, a trusted local reputation. In minutes you see the riskiest boxes, probably whether commuters will pay enough to cover a mobile mechanic, and you test those first. Now the limits. A new vaccine cannot ship a half-built MVP to learn; safety demands years of rigorous trials before anyone uses it. A deep hardware or space venture may need a large, up-front bet that cannot be sliced into weekly tests. And for a true breakthrough, early customers may not know what to make of it, so their feedback can mislead. Eric Ries himself frames lean as a response to uncertainty, not a cure for every kind of risk.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How many boxes does the Lean Canvas have, and who created it? 2) What question do you ask after filling it in? 3) Name two conditions under which lean startup methods work well. 4) Name one situation where the method fits poorly. 5) Why can early-customer feedback mislead for a radical product? Answers: 1) Nine boxes, created by Ash Maurya and adapted from Osterwalder's Business Model Canvas. 2) Which boxes are untested guesses rather than facts, so you know what to experiment on first. 3) When uncertainty is high and when experiments are cheap and fast to run. 4) When a single test is extremely costly or slow, such as a new medicine, or when the venture needs one large, indivisible bet. 5) Because customers may not yet understand a genuinely new product, so their early reactions do not reliably predict their later behavior.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the Lean Canvas as a document to perfect rather than a tool to spot risk and guide tests. Mistake: applying rapid experimentation where each test is slow, costly, or dangerous, and mistaking motion for progress. Mistake: swinging to the other extreme and dismissing lean entirely; even deep-technology teams can test demand, pricing, and usability cheaply around the parts that allow it. Mistake: forgetting that the method manages uncertainty, not every risk; some risks are financial or technical rather than questions about the market. Exit ticket: (a) What is the main job of the Lean Canvas? (b) Give one clear limit of the lean startup approach. Answers: to capture a business on one page and reveal which assumptions are the riskiest to test first; it fits poorly when a meaningful experiment would cost years, large sums, or safety, so the quick learning loop cannot run.
